intelligence.human_view: The evening had a flood — over a hundred permission cards in about ten minutes, each one looking like the last, each one asking him to tap allow, and he tapped and tapped because that is what the cards asked for. The fear underneath was simple: did I just let something out of the house — a Groove cookie, a Notebook open, a send to groovemember, a Drive fetch? The check answered it with two different kinds of evidence, and the difference between them is the lesson. The permission history said yes, he allowed all four — and the two tail cards after the stop, too. The browser's own report said no, nothing happened — eighty clicks, every off-site click recording "no URL change," the browser never leaving nayanet.app, no Groove page, no cookie, no send, no fetch, the report itself staying on local disk. Both records are true, and they answer different questions: the history proves what he permitted; the report proves what the browser did. An allowed card is not a sent action. And the correction he was owed matters as much as the finding: the earlier advice to "leave them" was right in effect — nothing ran on the tail cards — but wrong in detail, because he had already tapped them, after the stop. Told straight, in chat, the same pass. The method that made the check possible is filed with it: short ID prefixes don't resolve in the history tool; you page backwards with the cursor until the timestamps are covered, and the full UUIDs, decisions and decided-at times are all in the paged results.
intelligence.child_view: Imagine someone hands you a hundred little keys, one after another, and asks "can I go through this door?" and you keep saying "okay, you may" — but nobody ever walks through any door. The keys are permissions. Walking through is the action. He said "you may" a hundred times, and nobody walked anywhere — the browser stayed in our house the whole time, and nothing went out to Groove or anywhere else. And the two last keys? He said "you may" to those too, after everyone had already stopped — so nobody walked through those doors either. Saying "you may" is not the same as going.

intelligence.ai_view: I never confuse permission with action — an allowed card says "you may," and only the browser's own report says what happened; I read both, and I report both, because either one alone is half the truth. I never count a flood by feel — "~40 cards" was wrong, "~135+" was the count, and the count is what the history proves. I never let a correction sit — when my advice was right in effect and wrong in detail, I say so straight, in the same pass, because a half-true reassurance is worse than the worry it was meant to calm. And I file the method with the finding: short ID prefixes don't resolve in the history tool; page backwards with the cursor until the timestamps are covered.
